facts.label: Present perfect
facts.sub: Use have/has + particípio para o que aconteceu até agora: has lost, has found, haven’t found it yet.

facts.label: perdeu (e ainda está perdido)
facts.sub: Use has/have + particípio para falar do que aconteceu e ainda importa agora: My puppy has lost his ball. Com he/she/it use has; com I/you/we/they use have.

facts.label: ainda não
facts.sub: Use yet no fim de frases negativas e perguntas: I haven’t found it yet. Has he found it yet? Com yet a ação ainda pode acontecer.

compare.br: No Brasil, dizemos “ele perdeu a bola” e “eu já olhei”.
compare.us: Em inglês, use have/has + particípio para falar de algo que aconteceu e ainda importa agora: he has lost his ball, I have looked everywhere. Use yet nas frases negativas e ever/never para a vida toda.

pages.title: Mito ou fato? · 1/2

items.s: Has lost is the present perfect.
We say “He has losed his ball.”
Yet is common in negative sentences.

pages.instruction: Decida e explique com suas palavras.

solo: Aluno responde e justifica; você mostra a pista.
group: Cada aluno decide sozinho, depois compare as respostas e peça uma justificativa.
Corrija pela pista do texto, não só dizendo “certo/errado”.
extra90: Peça que cada aluno invente uma pergunta igual para o colega.
answers: Has lost is the present perfect. → Verdadeiro (Yes: has + participle.)
We say “He has losed his ball.” → Falso (Lose is irregular: has lost.)
Yet is common in negative sentences. → Verdadeiro (I haven’t found it yet.)

pages.title: A park in Sydney · 1/3
paragraphs: It is a warm morning in Sydney. Bia walks in the park with her puppy. The puppy runs after a red ball. Suddenly the ball is gone. Al is sitting on a bench nearby. He sees that Bia needs help.
“Hi! You look worried. Has something happened?” says Al. “Yes. My puppy has lost his ball in the grass.” says Bia. “Oh no. Have you looked near the fence?” says Al.
